chapter.name: Sound Waves: Characteristics and Applications
chapter.blurb: How sound is produced by vibrating sources and needs a medium to propagate; how it travels as a longitudinal, mechanical wave of compressions and rarefactions carrying energy; how a sound wave is described graphically and by its wavelength, frequency, time period, amplitude, intensity and speed; how humans perceive pitch and loudness within a limited audible range; and how reflection (echo, reverberation) and infrasonic/ultrasonic waves are put to use, from architecture to sonar and echolocation.

scope_in.item: Production of sound by vibration: source of sound, and examples from a plucked rubber band, human vocal cords, and animals such as grasshoppers and crickets
The tuning fork as a near-single-frequency source of sound, and confirming its vibration by touching a water surface
Propagation of sound through solids, liquids and gases; the meaning of a medium
The vacuum bell jar experiment showing sound needs a medium, and why astronauts cannot hear each other directly during a spacewalk
Sound as a series of alternating compressions and rarefactions (the slinky analogy and the oscillating-piston-in-a-tube model); the sound wave and its direction of propagation
Longitudinal waves versus transverse waves; sound as a mechanical wave
Sound as a form of energy; microphones and speakers as energy converters
Graphical representation of a sound wave (density against distance); crest, trough and average density
Wavelength, frequency and time period, and the relation nu = 1/T
Amplitude and intensity of a sound wave, and how intensity changes with distance from the source
Speed of sound, the relation v = lambda x nu, and how speed depends on the medium, temperature and humidity
Pitch, loudness, the human audible range, and infrasonic and ultrasonic waves
Tone, musical note, timbre and octave
Reflection of sound, echo, and the minimum distance/time needed to hear a clear echo
Reverberation and how auditoriums are designed to manage it
Applications of infrasonic and ultrasonic waves, including echolocation and sonar

concepts.name: Production of sound by vibration
concepts.description: Sound is produced whenever an object vibrates; the vibrating object is called the source of the sound, and once the vibration stops, so does the sound.
concepts.idea: Sound comes from a vibrating source, whether it is a plucked rubber band, a struck tuning fork, human vocal cords, or an insect rubbing its wings.
concepts.rule: Sound is produced by vibrating objects. Vibration is the periodic to-and-fro motion (oscillation) of an object about its rest position. A stretched rubber band that is plucked vibrates and produces sound; once it stops vibrating, the sound stops too. Pulling a stretched string, striking a metal object, or blowing air through the hollow pipe of a flute all make something vibrate, and it is this vibration that produces sound; the vibrating object or part is called the source of the sound. In humans and some other animals, sound is produced by the vibration of the vocal cords, tightly stretched muscular flaps located inside the voice box (larynx) in the throat; the tongue, lips, mouth and nasal cavity then help shape this sound into speech or music. Some animals, such as grasshoppers and crickets, produce sound by rubbing or striking certain body parts, such as their wings or legs, against each other. A tuning fork, a U-shaped metal bar with a stem, produces a near-single-frequency sound when one of its prongs is struck against a soft pad; touching a vibrating prong to a water surface makes ripples, confirming that the prong is vibrating even when this is too fast to see directly.
concepts.example: Stretching a rubber band across an open box and plucking it makes it vibrate and produce sound; the sound stops as soon as the rubber band stops vibrating.

questions.q: A classmate claims, 'Sound can sometimes be produced without anything vibrating.' Do you agree, based on this chapter? Justify your answer.

questions.q: Design a simple homemade activity, different from the rubber-band-and-box or tuning-fork activities in the chapter, that could show a younger student that sound is produced by vibration. Describe the setup and what should be observed.

s: Describes a workable setup

concepts.name: Propagation of sound: the need for a medium
concepts.description: Sound travels from its source to a listener only through a medium, solid, liquid or gas; it cannot propagate through a vacuum, a space with no matter at all.
concepts.idea: No medium, no sound: sound needs particles of matter to carry it, which is why it cannot cross empty (vacuum) space.
concepts.rule: The material through which sound travels is called a medium. Sound can propagate, or travel, through solids, liquids and gases. Pressing an ear to a desk while a friend gently knocks or scratches it (Activity 10.3) shows that sound travels through the solid desk; tapping two spoons together while they are submerged in water (Activity 10.4) shows that sound also travels through the liquid. A vacuum is a space that contains no medium (matter) at all. The vacuum bell jar experiment demonstrates that sound needs a medium: an electric bell is rung inside a sealed jar, and as air is pumped out with a vacuum pump, the sound becomes fainter and fainter; at near-vacuum, almost no sound can be heard even though the bell can still be seen ringing, and when air is let back in, the sound gradually returns to its original loudness. Because outer space is a near vacuum, sound cannot propagate there; this is why astronauts on a spacewalk cannot directly hear each other speak or hear sounds like metal clanking, and instead must communicate through special devices fitted into their spacesuits.
concepts.example: As air is pumped out of a bell jar containing a ringing electric bell, the sound grows fainter and fainter until it can barely be heard, even though the bell can still be seen ringing inside.

questions.a: This reasoning is wrong because a silent room is not a vacuum; a room is still full of air, which is a perfectly good medium for sound. The room is silent simply because there is no source producing sound at that moment, not because sound cannot propagate through it.

Water is a liquid and, like solids and gases, is a medium through which sound can and does propagate, as shown by Activity 10.4 where spoons tapped underwater are still heard; a vacuum is different because it has no matter (medium) at all, not because it cannot be breathed.
s: Identifies the flaw: breathability is not the relevant property

questions.q: Design a simple experiment, different from the vacuum bell jar or the spoons-in-water activity, that a classmate could use to convince a friend that sound needs a medium to travel, or that it can travel through more than one kind of medium. Describe the setup, what your friend should do, and what result would support your point.
questions.a: Any correctly reasoned original setup is acceptable, for example: tie a spoon to the middle of a length of string, wrap the ends of the string once around each index finger, put the fingertips gently in your ears, and let the spoon swing so it taps a table edge; the sound heard through the string (a solid medium) is much louder and clearer than through air alone. The friend should first listen to the spoon tapping the table through air only, and then repeat with the string against the ears, comparing loudness; a clearly louder, more solid-sounding tap through the string than through air alone would support the point that a solid can carry sound, sometimes better than air, so sound does depend on having a medium.
s: Describes a workable original setup
Describes what the friend should do to compare
States a result that would support sound needing/using a medium

concepts.name: Sound as a longitudinal mechanical wave, and the energy it carries
concepts.description: Sound travels through a medium as a series of compressions and rarefactions, a longitudinal, mechanical wave that carries energy without carrying the particles of the medium themselves along with it.
concepts.idea: Sound is an alternating pattern of denser (compression) and thinner (rarefaction) regions that moves through a medium, carrying energy, while each particle of the medium only oscillates about its own position.
concepts.rule: A slinky pushed and pulled at one end shows a disturbance, alternating regions where its turns are closer together and where they are more spread out, travelling along its length, even though a marked turn only oscillates about its own position and does not itself travel to the other end. Sound behaves similarly in a medium such as air: as a source (modelled as an oscillating piston in a tube) moves forward, it pushes nearby air particles together into a region of higher-than-average density called a compression; as it moves backward, it creates a region of lower-than-average density called a rarefaction. These regions travel forward through the medium as compressed or rarefied particles collide with and push their neighbours, even though the particles themselves only vibrate about their mean positions and do not travel with the disturbance. A sound wave is this disturbance of alternating compressions and rarefactions propagating through a medium, without the actual flow of the medium particles; the direction the wave travels is its direction of propagation. Waves in which the particles vibrate parallel to the direction of wave propagation, like sound, are called longitudinal waves, as opposed to transverse waves, where the particles vibrate perpendicular to the direction of propagation. Because sound needs a material medium to propagate, it is called a mechanical wave. When not confined to a tube, sound from a small source spreads out in all directions as a spherical wave. Sound also carries energy: in Activity 10.6, grains sprinkled on a stretched sheet jump when a loud sound reaches the sheet, because the sound energy makes the sheet vibrate. A microphone converts sound energy into electrical energy by using sound waves to vibrate a diaphragm, while a speaker does the reverse, using an electrical signal to vibrate a cone or diaphragm and produce sound.
concepts.example: In the slinky activity, pushing and pulling one end sends a disturbance of closely spaced and spread-out turns travelling along the slinky, while a marked turn only oscillates about its own position, just as air particles do when a compression or rarefaction of a sound wave passes through them.

questions.q: Using the slinky activity as an analogy, explain how sound travels from a vibrating tuning fork to your ear through the air, and clarify what does and does not actually travel across that distance.
questions.a: Just as pushing and pulling one end of a slinky sends a series of close-together and spread-out turns travelling along it without the turns themselves moving to the other end, a vibrating tuning fork disturbs the nearby air particles, creating alternating compressions (denser air) and rarefactions (less dense air). These compressions and rarefactions travel outward through the air to your ear through particle-to-particle collisions, carrying energy with them, while each individual air particle merely oscillates about its own position and does not travel all the way from the tuning fork to your ear.
s: Slinky analogy: disturbance travels, turns/particles do not

To show sound carries energy, observe the candle flame flickering or bending each time the loud sound reaches it, showing the sound has transferred enough energy to disturb the flame from a distance. To show sound is longitudinal, hold a light strip of paper directly in front of and facing the speaker cone; the paper should flutter back and forth in the same direction that the sound is travelling (toward and away from the speaker), rather than side to side, showing the air is being pushed parallel to the direction of propagation, as in a longitudinal wave.

Explains how it shows sound is longitudinal (parallel vibration)

concepts.name: Graphical representation of a sound wave: wavelength, frequency and time period
concepts.description: A sound wave can be shown as a graph of the medium density against distance, with crests and troughs, and is described by its wavelength, frequency and time period.
concepts.idea: On a density-versus-distance graph, the distance between two consecutive crests (or troughs) is the wavelength; how often, and how long, one full density oscillation takes at a fixed point define the frequency and time period.
concepts.rule: As a sound wave propagates, the density of the medium at any instant varies periodically with distance from the source; plotting this density against distance, with the average density marked as a horizontal dashed line, gives a wavy graph in which the highest point (maximum density, in a compression) is called the crest and the lowest point (minimum density, in a rarefaction) is called the trough. The wavelength of a sound wave, usually represented by the Greek letter lambda and measured in metres (its SI unit), is the distance between two consecutive crests, or between two consecutive troughs. At a fixed point in the medium, the density changes repeatedly from maximum to minimum and back to maximum (or the reverse); this change is called one complete oscillation. The frequency of the sound wave, represented by nu and measured in hertz (Hz, or per second), is the number of such density oscillations at a fixed point per unit time. The time period, represented by T and measured in seconds, is the time taken for one complete oscillation at a fixed point. Frequency and time period are inversely related: nu = 1/T. Everyday sounds usually contain a mixture of many frequencies, while a struck tuning fork or a whistle produces a sound that is close to a single frequency.
concepts.example: If a fixed point in a medium completes 10 density oscillations in 2 seconds, its frequency is 10/2 = 5 Hz and its time period is 1/5 = 0.2 s.

questions.a: (i) Since T = 1/nu, doubling the frequency nu halves the time period T; the wave completes each oscillation in half the time. s: Time period is halved, using T = 1/nu

s: Notes they are mathematically related (nu = 1/T), so one can be derived from the other

concepts.name: Amplitude, intensity and the speed of sound
concepts.description: The amplitude of a sound wave relates to the energy and loudness it carries, its intensity is the energy passing through a unit area per unit time and decreases with distance from the source, and its speed depends mainly on the medium it travels through.
concepts.idea: A larger amplitude wave carries more energy; that energy spreads out and weakens (lower intensity) with distance; and how fast the wave itself travels, its speed, depends chiefly on whether the medium is a solid, liquid or gas, and, for air, on temperature and humidity.
concepts.rule: The amplitude of a sound wave is the maximum change in the density of the medium in a compression (or rarefaction), compared to the average density; a larger change in density means a larger amplitude, and a wave with a larger amplitude carries more energy than one with a smaller amplitude, which is why striking a plate harder in Activity 10.6 makes the grains on the sheet jump higher. The intensity of sound is the amount of sound energy passing through a unit area, perpendicular to the direction of propagation, in a unit time; as a sound wave spreads out farther from a point source, the same total energy is spread over a larger area, so intensity decreases with distance, and sounds that start with a larger amplitude (and so more energy) can travel farther before their intensity falls to zero. The speed of sound is the distance a point on the wave, such as a crest or trough, travels in unit time; since the distance between two consecutive crests (the wavelength, lambda) is covered in one time period (T), the speed v = lambda/T, and since frequency nu = 1/T, this gives the key relation v = lambda x nu (speed = wavelength x frequency). The speed of sound depends on the medium: it travels fastest in solids, slower in liquids, and slowest in gases, roughly 4-5 times faster in water than in air and roughly 15-20 times faster in solids than in air. In air, the speed of sound also depends on temperature and humidity, increasing as either increases, for example from about 331 m/s at 0 degrees Celsius to about 344 m/s at 22 degrees Celsius; in most media, including air, the speed of sound depends only on the medium (and its conditions, such as temperature), not on the source or its frequency, so if a source frequency changes, the wavelength changes while the speed in that medium stays the same.
concepts.example: For a sound wave in air with a speed of 344 m/s and a frequency of 20 Hz, the wavelength is 344/20 = 17.2 m, using v = lambda x nu.

States what is measured (time to reach a fixed distance, used to find speed)

concepts.name: Human perception of sound, reflection, and ultrasonic/infrasonic applications
concepts.description: Humans perceive a sound wave's frequency as pitch and its amplitude as loudness, within an audible range of about 20 Hz to 20 kHz; sound reflects off surfaces to produce echoes and reverberation; and frequencies outside human hearing, infrasonic and ultrasonic waves, have important real-world applications such as sonar and echolocation.
concepts.idea: What is physically frequency and amplitude is what we perceive as pitch and loudness; reflected sound gives us echoes and reverberation; and infrasonic and ultrasonic waves, though inaudible to us, are put to work in nature and technology.
concepts.rule: How frequency is perceived by humans is called pitch: shrill sounds like a whistle have high pitch (generally higher frequency), while deep sounds like thunder have low pitch (generally lower frequency). Humans can hear only a limited range of frequencies, the audible range, roughly 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz (20 kHz), which varies from person to person and decreases with age; sound waves below 20 Hz are called infrasonic waves and those above 20 kHz are called ultrasonic waves, both inaudible to humans but detectable by some animals. A tone is a sound of a single frequency, such as from a tuning fork or oral whistling; a musical note, such as a plucked string, is a combination of a lowest frequency (the fundamental) and higher frequencies (overtones); timbre is the quality, arising from the pattern and intensity of overtones, that lets the same note sound different when played by different instruments; and an octave is the interval between two notes where one has double the frequency of the other. Loudness is how humans perceive the amplitude of a sound, commonly measured in decibels (dB); it is often used interchangeably with intensity in everyday language, but intensity is an objective, measurable quantity while loudness depends on the listener own hearing. Sound reflects off obstacles such as solids or liquids, following the same laws of reflection as light. An echo is a reflected sound heard again after the original, which is possible only if the reflected sound arrives at least about 0.1 s after the original, since a shorter gap cannot be distinguished by the brain; at a speed of sound of 340 m/s, this sets a minimum reflecting-surface distance of about 17 m for a clear echo. Reverberation is the persistence of sound in a large hall or auditorium due to multiple reflections arriving less than about 0.05 s apart; halls are designed with sound-absorbing surfaces to manage reverberation to a desirable level. Beyond the audible range, infrasonic waves are used to detect natural events such as earthquakes, volcanic eruptions and severe storms, since they travel long distances through air and the Earth; ultrasonic waves are used in medical imaging (ultrasonography), breaking kidney stones, industrial cleaning and welding, and detecting flaws inside metal. Echolocation is the use of reflected (ultrasonic) sound waves to locate objects, used by bats, dolphins and whales to navigate and hunt; sonar (sound navigation and ranging) applies the same principle underwater, sending ultrasonic waves and analysing their reflections to find the distance, direction and speed of objects such as submarines or shipwrecks.
concepts.example: A ship sonar signal sent into seawater at 1530 m/s returns after 0.90 s, so the reflecting object is at a distance of 1530 x (0.90/2) = 688.5 m.

questions.q: An architect adds thick curtains, soft upholstered chairs and sound-absorbing panels to a concert hall that previously sounded garbled. Explain, using the idea of reverberation, why this design choice helps.
questions.a: Hard, bare surfaces reflect sound strongly, causing many reflections to reach listeners with very short time gaps and build up as excessive reverberation, which garbles the sound; soft, porous surfaces like curtains, upholstered chairs and absorbing panels absorb sound instead of reflecting it, reducing the number and strength of these reflections so that reverberation is brought down to a desirable level.
s: Explains hard surfaces cause strong reflections/excess reverberation
Explains soft surfaces absorb sound and reduce this problem

questions.q: Compare how a bat uses echolocation to hunt at night with how a ship uses sonar to find a shipwreck, in terms of the type of wave used, the medium it travels through, and what is being measured from the reflected wave.
questions.a: Both echolocation and sonar work on the same basic principle: a source sends out ultrasonic waves, and the pattern and timing of the waves reflected back from an object are analysed to work out its position. A bat sends ultrasonic bursts through the air, which is the medium, and uses the echoes reflected from nearby obstacles or prey to judge their position in the dark; a ship's sonar sends ultrasonic waves into water, which is the medium, and analyses the reflected waves to determine the distance, direction and speed of underwater objects like a shipwreck. The key difference is mainly the medium (air for the bat, water for sonar) and the purpose (hunting/navigation for the bat, locating underwater objects for the ship), while the underlying physics, ultrasonic waves reflecting off obstacles and being analysed, is the same.
s: Both use ultrasonic waves reflected off objects (same underlying principle)
Bat: air as medium, used for hunting/avoiding obstacles
Sonar: water as medium, used to locate underwater objects like shipwrecks

questions.q: A student claims, 'Loudness and intensity are simply two different names for the exact same physical thing, so a louder sound and a more intense sound are identical in every way.' Evaluate this claim using the distinction made in the chapter.
questions.a: The claim is not fully correct; although loudness and intensity are often used interchangeably in everyday language and are related (both increase with a wave amplitude), the chapter distinguishes them: intensity is an objectively measurable physical quantity, the sound energy passing through a unit area per unit time, whereas loudness is subjective, depending on the individual listener hearing ability and perception, so two people can perceive the same intensity of sound as different loudness.
s: States the claim is not fully correct
Explains intensity is measurable/objective while loudness is subjective/perceptual

questions.q: Design a simple, safe plan to measure the minimum distance from a hard wall at which you and a friend can just start to hear a clear echo outdoors. Describe the equipment needed, the steps of your procedure, and how you would use your result together with the speed of sound in air to check it against the calculated value.
questions.a: Any correctly reasoned original plan is acceptable, for example: use a hard, flat wall in an open outdoor space, a loud but safe sound source such as clapping or a wooden clapper board, and a long measuring tape or a distance app. Starting close to the wall, clap once and listen; if no separate echo is heard, move back a measured distance and repeat, recording the distance at each attempt, until a clearly separate echo first becomes audible; note this shortest distance at which the echo is heard clearly. To check the result, use the calculation that at a speed of sound of about 340 m/s and a minimum audible time gap of 0.1 s, the minimum distance for a clear echo works out to about 17 m; compare the measured shortest distance to this 17 m value and discuss possible reasons for any difference, such as background noise or a less-than-ideal reflecting surface.
s: Describes a workable original procedure and equipment
Describes how the minimum echo distance would be found by trial
Compares the result to the calculated ~17 m using speed of sound and 0.1 s
